slides.title: Pricing in 2027 while churn rises
Key questions

claims.claim: Should Palisade raise prices at renewal in 2027 while churn is rising, and if so on which segments and by how much, to grow ARR at least 15% and keep net revenue retention above 100%?
evidence: Sub-questions: 1 Is rising churn a sign that customers reject our prices? 2 Which segments can take a price rise in 2027? 3 How much ARR does each option add, and does it meet the 2027 objectives? 4 How should the rise be sequenced, tested and monitored?
Decision maker: CEO Ravi Menon with the leadership team, approving the 2027 pricing plan
Success criteria: ARR grows at least 15% in 2027, from $86.0M to about $98.9M; Net revenue retention stays above 100% overall; The price change does not push churn up outside the promotion cohort
Timing: Leadership meeting, December 2026
Out of scope: Repackaging and new tiers; New-customer acquisition plan; Enterprise contracts renewing after 2027

slides.title: Executive summary

claims.claim: Raise mid-market and enterprise prices in 2027, and hold SMB until the promotion cohort is fixed and a price test passes
Churn is rising mainly in the 2025 SMB promotion cohort, not in the core customer base
evidence: Promotion customers explain about 91% of the rise in SMB churn
Onboarding is unlikely to cut SMB churn by much more than a third

claims.claim: Mid-market can likely take 10% and enterprise 7%, but SMB faces Inkwell's cheaper plan
evidence: A 10% higher mid-market price converted at 23.1%, against 23.6% (2024 test)
Our SMB win rate against Inkwell fell from 51% to 38% in a year

claims.claim: A targeted rise adds about $4.2M; 12% on every plan adds about $6.7M, not $10.3M, at more risk
evidence: Only 76% of ARR renews in 2027, so the CFO's $10.3M cannot all arrive
If retention holds, new customers need to add only about $0.8M to hit 15%

claims.claim: Decide in December, raise mid-market and enterprise from January, and test SMB first
evidence: Keep the 2,100 promotion customers out of the rise
Stop the SMB rollout if extra churn nears twice the 2023 response

slides.title: Why churn is rising
Churn is rising mainly in the 2025 promotion cohort, while the core base shows no sign of rejecting today's prices

claims.claim: 1a: The rise sits in SMB, and the board's blended churn figure hides where it comes from
evidence: 94% of customers lost each month in H1 2026 were SMB customers

claims.claim: 1b: The 2025 SMB promotion drives the rise: other SMB customers churn as they did a year ago
evidence: 91% of the rise in SMB monthly churn comes from the promotion cohort

claims.claim: 1c: Onboarding helps, but is unlikely to halve SMB churn; the discount ending appears to matter more
evidence: 32% is the most SMB churn could fall even if promotion customers churned like the rest

slides.title: 1a: Nearly all of the churn rise sits in SMB, where monthly churn climbed from 2.0% to 3.1% in a year

claims.claim: The churn problem is an SMB problem
evidence: Monthly logo churn H1 2025 / H1 2026: SMB 2.0% / 3.1%; Mid-market 0.6% / 0.8%; Enterprise 0.2% / 0.2%
94% of the customers lost each month in H1 2026 were SMB customers

claims.claim: SMB: monthly churn rose by 55% in a year, and SMB holds 80% of our customers
Mid-market: up from a low base, about 11 customers lost a month out of 1,350
Enterprise: flat, with fewer than one customer lost a month
evidence: Monthly logo churn as reported in the briefing pack, Table 1; customers lost a month = customers × monthly churn

slides.title: 1a: The board's churn figure has no definition, and neither blend of segment data reproduces it

claims.claim: Board dashboard figure is not defined; Define it first / Report churn by segment, with the promotion cohort shown on its own line
evidence: Board dashboard, Q2 2026: 1.4% (H1 2025), 2.3% (H1 2026); Not defined on the dashboard
The dashboard gives no periods for its two readings; we show them against H1 2025 and H1 2026

claims.claim: Share of all customers lost a month overstates: SMB is 80% of customers
evidence: 1.7% (H1 2025), 2.6% (H1 2026); Segment churn weighted by customers, mid-2026 mix

claims.claim: Logo churn weighted by ARR understates: SMB is a quarter of ARR
evidence: 0.8% (H1 2025), 1.2% (H1 2026); Segment churn weighted by segment ARR

claims.claim: SMB only: The number to manage
evidence: 2% (H1 2025), 3.1% (H1 2026); Monthly logo churn of the segment where the rise sits
Blends use mid-2026 customer and ARR counts for both periods, as the pack gives no mid-2025 mix

slides.title: 1b: The 2025 promotion explains about nine-tenths of the SMB churn rise; other SMB customers barely moved

claims.claim: Take the promotion out and the rise disappears
evidence: 91% of the rise in SMB monthly churn comes from the 2025 promotion cohort

claims.claim: Non-promotion SMB: nearly flat year on year, so the core SMB base is not leaving faster
All SMB: the jump comes from 2,100 promotion customers who are still in the base
Promotion cohort: 36% of SMB customers, but 56% of the SMB customers lost each month
evidence: the promotion share of customers lost uses the estimate on the next page

slides.title: 1b: Promotion customers churn at about 4.9% a month, more than twice the rate of other SMB customers

claims.claim: Estimated monthly churn of the promotion cohort is 4.9%, 2.3 times the rest
evidence: 182.9 SMB customers lost a month: 5,900 customers × 3.1% (Table 1)
− 79.8 non-promotion customers lost: 3,800 × 2.1% (section 6)
= 103.1 promotion customers lost a month
÷ 2,100 promotion customers still in the base

claims.claim: The estimate backs the cohort's churn out of the segment totals
evidence: Churn rates for H1 2026 apply to the mid-2026 customer counts in Table 1
The 2,100 promotion customers are the only SMB customers outside the non-promotion group
Customers who left before mid-2026 are not in the counts, so the estimate describes the cohort that remains
The pack reports no churn rate for the cohort itself; this is our estimate

slides.title: 1b: Price complaints cluster among promotion customers; other SMB churners cite price at about the 2025 level

claims.claim: The price shock was the discount ending, not our list price
evidence: Share citing "price / found a cheaper option": Promotion-cohort churners, H1 2026: 52%; All SMB churners, H1 2026: 34%; All SMB churners, H1 2025: 19%; Non-promotion SMB churners, H1 2026: 18%

claims.claim: Promotion churners: most left within two months of the 50% discount ending, when their bill doubled
All SMB, 2026: the higher share is a mix effect of promotion churners entering the survey
Non-promotion churners: the same share as all SMB churners a year earlier, despite Inkwell's $9 plan
evidence: The pack gives no survey response rates or sample sizes; shares are of churned customers who answered
No 2025 figure exists for non-promotion churners alone; H1 2025 SMB churners were almost all non-promotion, as the cohort was still on its discount

slides.title: 1c: Onboarding is unlikely to halve SMB churn: even matching other customers' churn would cut it by a third

claims.claim: The goal sits below anything SMB has shown
evidence: SMB monthly churn: SMB today, H1 2026: 3.1%; If promotion customers churned like the rest: 2.1%; Customer Success goal: half: 1.55%
32% largest possible cut in SMB churn
Customer Success view (pack, section 10): "An onboarding programme will halve SMB churn within two quarters"

claims.claim: Best case: SMB falls only to the non-promotion rate
evidence: A bound from our model: it assumes onboarding brings promotion customers to the non-promotion rate; activating the other customers who never reach five documents could add a little more

claims.claim: Goal: below the 1.8% SMB had before the 2023 rise
Fund onboarding, but do not bank a halving of churn in the 2027 plan

slides.title: 1c: Activation explains only about 30% of the promotion cohort's extra churn; the discount ending likely drove the rest

claims.claim: Activation explains about 30% of the promotion cohort's extra churn
evidence: 2.9% churn the cohort's 41% activation rate predicts, with three times the churn for customers who never activated
− 2.1% non-promotion SMB churn, H1 2026
= 0.8 pp extra churn that activation explains
÷ 2.8 pp the cohort's total extra churn: 4.9% against 2.1%
= 30% share of the extra churn that better onboarding could reach

claims.claim: The split rests on the pack's activation evidence
evidence: Customers who sent fewer than five documents in month one churn at three times the rate of the rest, in both groups (section 9 of the pack)
Activated customers churn at the same rate in the promotion cohort and in other cohorts
Non-promotion SMB customers activate at the 72% rate of other cohorts
Activated = sent at least five documents in the first month (pack, section 6); activated SMB churn implied at 1.35% a month

claims.claim: Whatever activation does not explain is attributed to the end of the 50% discount, since most leavers went within two months of it
evidence: The pack shows timing, not cause: most leavers went within two months of the discount ending

slides.title: Why churn is rising
Mid-market and enterprise can take a rise in 2027; SMB cannot yet, with Inkwell undercutting its plan

claims.claim: 2a: Mid-market: Raise 10% at renewal / More than half of all 2027 renewals, at the lowest risk
evidence: ARR renewing in 2027: $34.9M
A 10% rise did not dent conversion in 2024; customers stay for integrations and the audit trail

claims.claim: 2b: Enterprise: Raise up to the 7% cap
evidence: ARR renewing in 2027: $9.6M
Most contracts cap yearly rises at 7%, and most ARR renews after 2027

claims.claim: 2c: SMB: Hold, and test first
evidence: ARR renewing in 2027: $21M
Inkwell's Starter plan is far cheaper and our win rate against it fell; the 2023 rise is the only guide

slides.title: 2a: Mid-market buyers barely reacted when the 2024 test raised list prices 10%

claims.claim: 10% higher list price for new mid-market sign-ups, 2024 test: conversion 23.1% against 23.6% for the control group
evidence: A 2.1% relative drop, not statistically significant
Three-month test, new sign-ups only
Existing customers at renewal were not tested

claims.claim: 112% mid-market net revenue retention, trailing 12 months: expansion outweighs losses
evidence: Integrations and the audit trail are the main reasons to stay (advisory board, 2026)
Both are costly to replace mid-contract

claims.claim: 0.8% mid-market monthly logo churn, H1 2026: 26% of the SMB rate
evidence: Up from 0.6% in H1 2025, from a low base
Inkwell not seen in deals above 200 seats

claims.claim: The test ran on new sign-ups, so how existing customers react at renewal is an open question (appendix)

slides.title: 2a: Mid-market is where a 2027 rise pays most: it holds $34.9M of renewing ARR at low churn

claims.claim: SMB: All renews, but churn is highest
evidence: ARR $21M; Monthly churn H1 2026 3.1%; NRR 94%; ARR renewing in 2027 100%; Renewing ARR $21M

claims.claim: Mid-market: Largest and safest base
evidence: ARR $41M; Monthly churn 0.8%; NRR 112%; ARR renewing in 2027 85%; Renewing ARR $34.9M

claims.claim: Enterprise: Safe, but little renews
evidence: ARR $24M; Monthly churn 0.2%; NRR 118%; ARR renewing in 2027 40%; Renewing ARR $9.6M
Net revenue retention is trailing 12 months; renewing ARR = segment ARR × share renewing in 2027 (pack, section 8)

slides.title: 2b: Enterprise cannot take 12% across the board: only 40% of its ARR renews in 2027, and 60% is capped at 7%

claims.claim: A 7% rise is the most enterprise can give in 2027
evidence: 40% share of enterprise ARR renews in 2027: $9.6M of $24.0M; The rest renews later on multi-year terms
60% share of enterprise ARR capped at 7% a year: Caps apply at each renewal; A 12% ask would breach them
7% Yearly rise allowed in capped contracts

claims.claim: Renewal timing: most enterprise ARR is out of reach until 2028 or later
Caps: 7% is the ceiling for most contracts; we propose it for the uncapped rest too, to keep one message
Retention: enterprise churn is flat at 0.2% a month and NRR is 118%, so 7% is low risk
ARR from 7% on 2027 enterprise renewals: $0.7M
evidence: $24.0M × 40% renewing × 7%
The pack does not say how much of the 2027 renewals is capped; we assume the same 60% as for all enterprise ARR

slides.title: 2c: Our SMB plan costs 67% more than Inkwell's Starter, and our win rate against Inkwell fell from 51% to 38%

claims.claim: Inkwell's Starter plan undercuts every Palisade plan
evidence: List price, $ per user per month, 2026: Inkwell Starter 9; Palisade SMB 15; Inkwell Pro 24; Palisade Business 29

claims.claim: Since Starter launched, we lose more SMB deals where Inkwell is considered
evidence: −13 pp
SMB win rate where Inkwell was considered: H1 2025 51%; H1 2026 38%
Inkwell launched Starter in October 2025; it has not been seen in deals above 200 seats (pack, section 7)

claims.claim: A higher SMB list price now would widen the gap to Inkwell exactly where we are losing deals

slides.title: 2c: The 2023 SMB rise was followed by a six-month churn spike, and that was before Inkwell's cheaper plan existed

claims.claim: The spike, not the settled rate, was the main cost
evidence: SMB monthly churn around the 2023 rise of 8%: Before the rise 1.8%; Six months after 2.3%; After it settled 1.9%
3.6% of SMB customers lost in the first year beyond the pre-rise rate
First-year extra loss = 0.5 percentage points above 1.8% for six months + 0.1 above it for six more

claims.claim: Spike: churn ran 28% above its old rate for six months
Settled: churn stayed slightly above the old rate, a lasting cost
Today: Inkwell's $9 plan means the 2023 response may understate what a rise would trigger now
evidence: The non-promotion SMB base today churns at 2.1% a month (1b), above the 1.8% of 2023

slides.title: Why churn is rising
A targeted rise captures most of the realistic price value and spares the customers most likely to leave

claims.claim: 3a: The CFO's 12% plan adds about $6.7M, not $10.3M, once renewal timing, caps and SMB churn are counted
evidence: 76% of ARR renews in 2027 and can take a new price at all

claims.claim: 3b: 10% on mid-market and 7% on enterprise renewals adds about $4.2M with little churn risk
evidence: $34.9M of mid-market ARR renews in 2027, the base most of the rise sits on

claims.claim: 3c: An 8% SMB rise nets about $0.7M and turns negative if churn reacts more than twice as hard as in 2023
evidence: $16.6M of non-promotion SMB ARR an 8% rise would apply to

claims.claim: 3d: With today's retention, the targeted plan leaves only about $0.8M of the 15% target to new customers
evidence: 109.3% ARR-weighted net revenue retention today, above the 100% floor

slides.title: 3a: The 12% plan would add about $6.7M in 2027, not $10.3M, before any extra promotion-cohort losses

claims.claim: Renewal timing is the largest correction
evidence: Waterfall, $M: 12% on all ARR 10.3; ARR not renewing in 2027 −2.46; Enterprise caps at 7% −0.29; SMB churn response −0.85; 12% plan, 2027 6.72
24% of the CFO's figure cannot arrive in 2027, because that ARR renews later
The CFO's $10.3M is 12% of all $86.0M of ARR (pack, section 4)

claims.claim: Not renewing: 15% of mid-market and 60% of enterprise ARR renew after 2027, at today's price
Caps: most enterprise contracts stop at 7%, a small correction
How the 12% plan's 2027 value is built
evidence: $7.9M 12% on the $65.5M of ARR renewing in 2027
− $0.3M 7% cap on 60% of enterprise renewals
− $0.8M SMB ARR lost at the 2023 churn response
= $6.7M ARR the 12% plan adds by the end of 2027

claims.claim: SMB churn: uses the 2023 response to 8%, so it is a floor for a 12% rise against Inkwell
evidence: Assumptions in the appendix

slides.title: 3b: Raising mid-market 10% and enterprise 7% at renewal adds about $4.2M, with mid-market carrying most of it

claims.claim: The targeted plan adds $4.2M, 62% of the 12% plan's value, without touching SMB
evidence: $3.5M 10% on $34.9M of mid-market ARR renewing in 2027, the rise tested in 2024 (2a)
+ $0.7M 7% on $9.6M of enterprise ARR renewing in 2027, the contract cap (2b)
= $4.2M ARR the targeted plan adds by the end of 2027
÷ $6.7M realistic value of 12% on every plan (3a)

claims.claim: The estimate counts only what the evidence supports
evidence: Mid-market renewals in 2027 take the 10% rise tested on new sign-ups in 2024
Enterprise renewals in 2027 take 7%, the cap in 60% of enterprise ARR; uncapped contracts are held to the same level
No change in mid-market or enterprise churn, as in the 2024 test; existing customers at renewal were not tested
SMB list prices stay flat in 2027 unless the H1 2027 test passes; no SMB gain is counted

slides.title: 3b: The targeted plan gives up part of the across-the-board gain but spares the customers most likely to leave

claims.claim: 12% on every plan: Highest ARR, highest churn risk
evidence: ARR added in 2027 $6.7M; Every customer, including the 2,100 promotion customers; SMB premium over Inkwell Starter 87%

claims.claim: Targeted: 10% mid-market, 7% enterprise: Recommended / About $0.5M of the 12% plan's gain would come from promotion customers who already leave fastest
evidence: ARR added in 2027 $4.2M; Customers with the lowest churn and highest retention; SMB premium 67%

claims.claim: Hold all prices: Misses the price lever entirely
evidence: No price gain; Nobody; SMB premium 67%

claims.claim: What the targeted plan gives up: $2.6M ARR given up in return for no rise on SMB
evidence: $6.7M 12% on every plan (3a) − $4.2M targeted plan (3b) = $2.6M
SMB premium = SMB plan list price ÷ Inkwell Starter price − 1; $15 today, $16.80 after a 12% rise

slides.title: 3c: An 8% SMB rise nets about $0.7M, and loses money if churn reacts over twice as hard as in 2023

claims.claim: Net ARR from an 8% rise on non-promotion SMB is $0.7M; it is gone at about 2.1 times the 2023 response
evidence: $16.6M non-promotion SMB ARR; promotion customers are left out
× 8% rise at renewal, the size of the 2023 rise
= $1.3M gross ARR in the first year
− $0.7M ARR lost if 3.6% more customers leave in year one, as in 2023 (2c)
= $0.7M net ARR

claims.claim: A thin margin, which is why SMB is tested before any rollout
evidence: The 8% rise applies to the 3,800 non-promotion SMB customers only; promotion customers keep today's price
The churn response repeats the 2023 pattern (2c), counted over the first twelve months
Lost customers would have paid the new price; ARR is counted at run-rate
Break-even extra loss = $1.33M ÷ ($16.6M × 1.08) = 7.4% of customers in year one
Sensitivity to the churn response in the appendix

slides.title: 3d: If retention holds, the targeted rise brings ARR within about $0.8M of the 15% target, leaving that to new customers

claims.claim: $0.8M still needed from new customers in 2027
evidence: $12.9M ARR the 15% growth target adds: $86.0M × 15%
− $7.98M added by existing customers at today's 109.3% ARR-weighted retention
− $4.2M added by 10% on mid-market and 7% on enterprise renewals (3b)

claims.claim: Both objectives hold if 2027 retention matches the last 12 months
evidence: Existing customers keep the trailing-12-month net revenue retention of each segment in 2027 (94%, 112%, 118%)
That retention contained no list-price rise, so the targeted rise comes on top of it
The targeted rise adds $4.2M at full run-rate (3b)
New-customer ARR is what is left to reach the target; the pack has no figure for 2026 new bookings
With the targeted rise, net revenue retention would be about 114%, well above the 100% floor
SMB retention of 94% already includes the promotion cohort's losses; if they ease, the gap shrinks
The pack states the target from $86.0M; the bridge applies one year of trailing retention to that base, so the result is sensitive to 2027 retention

slides.title: Why churn is rising
Decide in December, raise mid-market and enterprise from January, and test SMB before any rollout later in the year

claims.claim: 2027 pricing plan, by quarter
evidence: Dec 2026: Leadership decision; Q2 2027: SMB test read-out
Mid-market: 10% at each renewal, with value story
Enterprise: 7% at renewal, within contract caps
SMB, non-promotion: 8% test on part of renewals; Roll out only if test passes
Promotion cohort: Activation and save programme, no rise
Reporting: One churn definition, by segment

claims.claim: One read-out in Q2 decides SMB, so the risk of a wider rise stays with a test group

slides.title: 4a: An activation programme gives the promotion cohort a reason to stay before any price rise reaches it

claims.claim: Lift promotion customers to the five-document mark, and keep them off the 2027 price rise
evidence: ARR in the promotion cohort to protect: $4.4M
Reach: Contact promotion customers below five documents a month; Offer guided set-up of their first workflows
Protect: Exclude the cohort from any 2027 list-price rise; Track its churn on its own line in reporting
Review: Read cohort churn monthly against 4.9%; Stop the programme if churn does not fall by Q2 2027
Owner Head of Customer Success · Timing Dec 2026 – Q2 2027

slides.title: 4b: A first-half SMB test settles whether non-promotion customers can take a rise now that Inkwell is in the market

claims.claim: Raise 8% on a random part of non-promotion SMB renewals and compare churn with a held-back group
evidence: Non-promotion SMB ARR the test decides on: $16.6M
Design: Random split of non-promotion SMB renewals into test and control; Promotion customers excluded
Measure: Extra churn in the test group against control, monthly; Win rate in deals where Inkwell is considered
Decide: Roll out in H2 only if extra churn stays well below 7.4% for the year; Otherwise hold SMB prices for 2027
Owner CFO with Head of Growth · Timing Q1 – Q2 2027

slides.title: Four risks need an owner before January, led by mid-market renewals reacting worse than new sign-ups did

claims.claim: Mid-market renewals: Existing customers react worse than new sign-ups in the 2024 test — Largest risk / It carries most of the $4.2M, and renewal behavior was never tested
evidence: How we reduce it: Lead with integrations and audit trail; watch the first quarter of renewals; Owner: Head of Sales

claims.claim: Promotion cohort: Cohort keeps leaving at about 4.9% a month
evidence: Activation programme; no rise for the cohort; Owner: Head of Customer Success; Watch point: Report on its own line

claims.claim: Inkwell: Inkwell moves up into mid-market deals
evidence: Track Inkwell presence in deals above 200 seats; Owner: Head of Sales; Watch point: Watch deal mix

claims.claim: Churn reporting: The board keeps reading an undefined churn figure
evidence: One definition, by segment, from Q1 2027; Owner: CFO; Watch point: Fix in December

slides.title: Five numbers will tell leadership by mid-2027 whether the pricing plan is working

claims.claim: 2027 pricing scorecard, latest value and guardrail
evidence: Mid-market monthly logo churn: Today 0.8%; Stays at or below today's level after the rise
Net revenue retention, all customers: 109.3%; Above 100%, the objective
Promotion-cohort monthly churn: 4.9%; Falls toward the non-promotion rate
SMB test: extra customers lost: 3.6%; Well below twice the 2023 response
SMB win rate where Inkwell is considered: 38%; No further fall
103.1 promotion customers lost a month (1b) ÷ 2,100 promotion customers = 4.9% promotion-cohort churn
Promotion-cohort churn is a team estimate (1b); the 2023 response is the first-year extra loss after the 8% rise (2c)

slides.title: Three branches were left out on purpose: two lack data in the pack, and one is outside our control
BACKUP: Three branches were left out on purpose: two lack data in the pack, and one is outside our control

claims.claim: Repackaging: New tiers or usage-based pricing would lift ARR more than list-price rises
evidence: The pack has no plan-mix or usage data; a candidate for the 2028 review

claims.claim: Inkwell's next move: Inkwell will cut prices again or move into mid-market
evidence: Outside our influence; tracked through win rate and deal mix (4c)

claims.claim: New-customer growth: Acquisition alone can carry the 15% target
evidence: Out of scope for a pricing decision; no bookings data in the pack (3d)

slides.title: BACKUP: Mid-market holds nearly half of ARR, while SMB holds four in five customers

claims.claim: Segment fact base, mid-2026
evidence: SMB: 5,900 customers; $21M ARR; 24% ARR share; churn 3.1%; NRR 94%; 1–50 employees; self-serve, monthly or annual plans
Mid-market: 1,350; $41M; 48%; 0.8%; 112%; 51–1,000 employees; annual contracts
Enterprise: 150; $24M; 28%; 0.2%; 118%; Over 1,000 employees; mostly multi-year contracts
ARR per customer: about $3.6K in SMB, $30.4K in mid-market and $160K in enterprise

slides.title: BACKUP: Four churn terms need one meaning each before the board sees the next dashboard

claims.claim: Definitions used in this deck
evidence: Monthly logo churn: Share of a segment's customers lost in a month, averaged over the half-year (Pack, Table 1)
Net revenue retention: ARR from customers a year ago, today, divided by their ARR then; trailing 12 months (Pack, Table 1)
Promotion cohort: SMB customers who joined February–August 2025 at 50% off for six months (Pack, section 6)
Activated customer: Sent at least five documents in the first month (Pack, section 6)

slides.title: BACKUP: The value estimates rest on five planning assumptions for leadership to confirm

claims.claim: Planning assumptions behind section 3
evidence: Share of ARR renewing in 2027: 76%; Renewal shares by segment (pack, section 8)
Mid-market rise at renewal: 10%; The rise tested on new sign-ups in 2024
Enterprise rise at renewal: 7%; Contract cap on 60% of enterprise ARR
SMB extra customers lost in year one: 3.6%; The 2023 response to 8%, used for any SMB rise
ARR-weighted retention in 2027: 109.3%; Trailing 12 months, held flat

slides.title: BACKUP: An SMB price rise stays positive only up to about twice the 2023 churn response

claims.claim: Net ARR from 8% on non-promotion SMB by churn response, first 12 months
evidence: As in 2023: 3.6% extra lost; $0.7M; Base case (3c)
One and a half times 2023: 5.4%; $0.3M
Twice 2023: 7.2%; $0.03M; About break-even
Three times 2023: 10.8%; −$0.6M; Loses ARR
$1.3M gross ARR from 8% on $16.6M − $0.7M ARR lost at the 2023 response, times the row's multiple = $0.7M net ARR, base case

slides.title: BACKUP: Three open questions remain, and the plan tests each one before betting on it

claims.claim: SMB price sensitivity with Inkwell: Decides whether SMB can take any rise in 2027
evidence: H1 2027 renewal test with a control group (4b)

claims.claim: Can the promotion cohort be activated? Decides how much of the cohort's ARR survives
evidence: Activation programme with a Q2 stop rule (4a)

claims.claim: Do renewals react like new sign-ups? Decides whether mid-market delivers its share of the rise
evidence: First-quarter renewal read-out (4c)

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Raise mid-market and enterprise prices in 2027, and hold SMB until the promotion cohort is fixed and a price test passes: decide in December, raise mid-market 10% and enterprise 7% (within contract caps) at renewal from January, keep the 2,100 promotion customers out of the rise with an activation and save programme, and test 8% on part of non-promotion SMB renewals, rolling out only if the test passes (stop if extra churn nears twice the 2023 response).

alternatives_considered.treatment: Adds about $6.7M, not $10.3M, once renewal timing, caps and SMB churn are counted; "Highest ARR, highest churn risk"; every customer including the 2,100 promotion customers carries the rise; SMB premium over Inkwell Starter rises to 87%. Not recommended.
Recommended. Adds about $4.2M (62% of the 12% plan's value) with customers with the lowest churn and highest retention; gives up $2.6M in return for no rise on SMB.
No price gain; "Misses the price lever entirely".

Nets about $0.7M and turns negative if churn reacts more than about twice as hard as in 2023; "A thin margin, which is why SMB is tested before any rollout"; tested in H1 2027, rolled out in H2 only if extra churn stays well below 7.4%.

alternatives_considered.option: Onboarding programme to halve SMB churn (Customer Success view)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Onboarding is unlikely to halve SMB churn; best case cuts it by 32%. "Fund onboarding, but do not bank a halving of churn in the 2027 plan".
Rejected: only 40% of enterprise ARR renews in 2027 and 60% is capped at 7%; a 12% ask would breach the caps. 7% proposed for uncapped contracts too, to keep one message.
Left out on purpose: the pack has no plan-mix or usage data; a candidate for the 2028 review.

alternatives_considered.option: New-customer growth: acquisition alone can carry the 15% target
alternatives_considered.treatment: Left out: out of scope for a pricing decision; no bookings data in the pack.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Synthetic benchmark data; all figures from the briefing pack or team estimates
The board dashboard churn figure is not defined and gives no periods for its two readings
Blends use mid-2026 customer and ARR counts for both periods, as the pack gives no mid-2025 mix
Promotion-cohort churn of 4.9% is a team estimate; the pack reports no churn rate for the cohort itself; customers who left before mid-2026 are not in the counts
The pack gives no survey response rates or sample sizes; no 2025 figure exists for non-promotion churners alone
Onboarding bound assumes onboarding brings promotion customers to the non-promotion rate; activating other customers who never reach five documents could add a little more
Whatever activation does not explain is attributed to the end of the 50% discount; the pack shows timing, not cause
The 2024 mid-market test ran on new sign-ups only for three months; existing customers at renewal were not tested; how existing customers react at renewal is an open question
The pack does not say how much of the 2027 enterprise renewals is capped; we assume the same 60% as for all enterprise ARR
Inkwell's $9 plan means the 2023 response may understate what a rise would trigger now; SMB churn correction in the 12% plan is a floor
No change in mid-market or enterprise churn assumed, as in the 2024 test
SMB churn response repeats the 2023 pattern; lost customers would have paid the new price; ARR counted at run-rate
Existing customers keep trailing-12-month NRR of each segment in 2027 (94%, 112%, 118%); result is sensitive to 2027 retention
The pack has no figure for 2026 new bookings

Five planning assumptions for leadership to confirm: 76% of ARR renewing in 2027; 10% mid-market rise; 7% enterprise rise; 3.6% SMB extra customers lost in year one; 109.3% ARR-weighted retention held flat

Risks: mid-market renewals react worse than new sign-ups (largest risk); promotion cohort keeps leaving at about 4.9% a month; Inkwell moves up into mid-market deals; board keeps reading an undefined churn figure
Open questions: SMB price sensitivity with Inkwell; whether the promotion cohort can be activated; whether renewals react like new sign-ups
next_steps: Approve 10% on mid-market and 7% on enterprise renewals from January 2027 — CEO and leadership team — Dec 2026
Adopt one churn definition by segment, with the promotion cohort on its own line — CFO — Dec 2026
Launch the promotion-cohort activation programme, with a Q2 stop rule — Head of Customer Success — Jan 2027
Design and start the SMB renewal price test with a control group — CFO with Head of Growth — Q1 2027
Read out the SMB test and decide the H2 rollout — CEO and CFO — Jul 2027
normalized.extraction_notes: Slides 4, 13, 20 and 27 are contents/section-divider slides. The extraction gives each of them the title "Why churn is rising", which looks like the first section's name pulled in as the title; the titles are copied as extracted. Slide 33 is the appendix contents page and repeats slide 34's title. Chart values were given as decimals and are written here as percentages, e.g. 0.031 → 3.1%. The waterfall series on slide 22 (base/ARR added) is shown as step values. The extraction contains no images. References to section "4c" (slides 34 and 39) point to no slide with that label.
